The Hacker News

An attacker drained 1,196 Bitcoin addresses in 41 minutes on July 30, taking 1,082.65 BTC worth about $70.2 million at the time. Galaxy Research mapped the sweep and tied it to a firmware flaw in Coldcard, the Bitcoin-only hardware wallet made by Canadian firm Coinkite. Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,

SecurityEvent

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Active Storage crafted image upload to libvips variant endpoints (CVE-2026-66066) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts unauthenticated traffic to Rails Active Storage upload and variant/representation endpoints, the exploitation surface for CVE-2026-66066 (KindaRails2Shell) where a crafted image drives libvips into an arbitrary-file-read. Surfaces sources that both submit uploads and request server-side image processing so an analyst can triage the file-read primitive. Rationale: Uses the canonical Rails Active Storage route prefixes (/rails/active_storage/direct_uploads, /representations/, /blobs/, /disk/) — corroborated by Rapid7/Ethiack as the direct-upload + variant-processing surface. Technical PoC strings were withheld by the researchers, so this is a triage hunt on the exploit surface rather than a signature. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve-2026-66066 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-rails-flaw-could-let.html
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate users uploading avatars/profile pictures and viewing generated thumbnails
  • Load/synthetic monitoring hitting upload endpoints
  • CDN or image-proxy warming Active Storage representations in bulk
  • Mobile app clients using direct_uploads at high volume
  • Security scanners (internal ASM/DAST) probing the same routes
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(SrcIpAddr) and SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the raw requests for the top source IPs — check whether they are unauthenticated, whether upload requests are immediately followed by representation/variant requests, and whether responses are anomalously sized (leaked file content). 2) Contain: if libvips <8.13 or the app is unpatched (Rails <7.2.3.2/8.0.5.1/8.1.3.1), block the source at the WAF/reverse-proxy and enable VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host to UC 'Rails worker sensitive-file access' and 'Rails worker spawning shell/network child' to confirm file-read and RCE.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/rails/active_storage/"
| where Url has_any ("/representations/", "/blobs/", "/direct_uploads", "/disk/")
| summarize Requests = count(), Methods = make_set(HttpMethod, 10), Statuses = make_set(HttpStatusCode, 10), SampleUrls = make_set(Url, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, HttpHostName
| order by LastSeen desc

Rails/Ruby worker reading secret_key_base and credential files post-upload (CVE-2026-66066) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the Rails application process (ruby/puma/unicorn/passenger) accessing sensitive secret and environment files — the credential-access step of CVE-2026-66066 where the libvips arbitrary-file-read is used to exfiltrate secret_key_base, master.key, credentials.yml.enc, .env and /proc/self/environ. High-fidelity because a running web worker should not be reading these at request time. Rationale: Ties the standard Rails secret paths named in the article (secret_key_base, master.key, database/cloud creds in the process environment) to the app-server process identity — a Rails worker reading /proc/self/environ or master.key at runtime is the direct fingerprint of the file-read primitive being abused. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/critical-rails-flaw-could-let.html • https://socprime.com/blog/cve-2026-66066-critical-rails-flaw-exposes-server-files-via-image-uploads/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Normal app boot reading config/master.key and credentials.yml.enc during initialization (baseline once per deploy/restart)
  • dotenv gems loading .env at startup
  • Config-management/CI tooling templating credential files
  • APM/observability agents enumerating process environment
  • Developer console (rails c) sessions on a jump host
Suppression filter
| where ActionType != "FileCreated" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "rails console" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "assets:precompile"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the access is at request-serving time (not process boot) and correlate the host/timestamp with UC1 Active Storage upload traffic within the same window. 2) Contain: treat secret_key_base, DB and Active Storage credentials as compromised — rotate them, rotate the Rails master key, and patch to Rails 7.2.3.2/8.0.5.1/8.1.3.1 with libvips ≥8.13. 3) Hunt: search for forged session cookies / anomalous authenticated sessions and pivot to UC3 for shell/network children of the worker.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "bundle", "rails")
| where FileName in~ ("credentials.yml.enc", "master.key", "environ", ".env")
    or FolderPath has_any ("/config/credentials", "/proc/self/environ")
| where FolderPath !startswith "/tmp/" and FolderPath !has "/active_storage/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "bundle", "rails")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/config/credentials.yml.enc", "/config/master.key", "/config/credentials/", "/proc/self/environ")
    or TargetFileName =~ ".env"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessId, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rails app worker spawning shell or network child (KindaRails2Shell RCE) AIInstallation High
Detects the Rails/Ruby application server (puma/unicorn/passenger/ruby) spawning an unexpected shell or network client (sh, bash, curl, wget, nc, python, ruby -e) — the RCE execution stage where a forged, secret_key_base-signed serialized payload drives insecure deserialization into command execution on the host. Rationale: A web application worker (puma/unicorn/passenger/ruby) is not expected to fork shells or curl/wget at runtime; pairing that specific parent set with shell/network children is the highest-fidelity signal of the deserialization-to-RCE endgame the article and Akamai describe. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://ethiack.com/info-hub/research/kindarails2shell-rails-rce-cve-2026-66066
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rails app legitimately shelling out to ImageMagick/ffmpeg/git via system() for background jobs
  • Sidekiq/Resque workers running rake tasks that invoke curl/bash
  • Health-check or entrypoint scripts (bash) launched by the app container
  • Deploy hooks calling shell from within the app process
  • Ruby scripts using backticks for legitimate ops tooling
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert", "identify", "vipsthumbnail", "ffmpeg", "/rake", "sidekiq", "healthcheck"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line — reverse-shell one-liners, curl to unknown IPs, or writes to /tmp are strong TP indicators; benign image/rake tooling is FP. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the spawned process tree, and treat app secrets as compromised (rotate secret_key_base + all DB/cloud creds). 3) Hunt: pull outbound connections from the child, correlate back to the originating Active Storage upload (UC1) and credential-file reads (UC2), and search other Rails hosts for the same parent→child pattern.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "rails", "bundle")
| where FileName in~ ("sh", "bash", "dash", "curl", "wget", "nc", "ncat", "python", "python3", "perl")
    or (FileName in~ ("ruby") and ProcessCommandLine has "-e ")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ruby", "puma", "unicorn", "passenger", "rails", "bundle")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh", "/bash", "/dash", "/curl", "/wget", "/nc", "/ncat", "/python", "/perl")
    or (ActingProcessName has "/ruby" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-e ")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposure hunt: hosts with vulnerable libvips / Rails Active Storage (CVE-2026-66066) AIExploitation High
Surfaces internet-facing hosts still exposed to CVE-2026-66066 — libvips before 8.13 (which cannot disable the unfuzzed operations at all) or unpatched Rails Active Storage. Drives pre-exploitation prioritization since public PoCs are already circulating. Rationale: Directly keys on the article's named CVE (CVE-2026-66066) and the libvips 8.13 fix floor; scoping to internet-facing hosts turns the vuln feed into an actionable, prioritized exposure list ahead of the disclosed public PoCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-kindarails2shell-cve-2026-66066-critical-arbitrary-file-read-and-possible-remote-code-execution-in-ruby-on-rails/ • https://www.linuxcompatible.org/story/rails-7232-8051-and-8131-active-storage-security-patch-targets-cve202666066
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts that use ImageMagick (not libvips) as the Active Storage processor — not actually exploitable
  • Apps that do not accept untrusted image uploads (internal-only) — lower real risk
  • TVM version-string mismatch flagging a backported/distro-patched libvips as vulnerable
  • Rails 6.x using Active Storage defaults (not affected) still flagged by generic version match
  • Decommissioned/quarantined hosts still in inventory
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each flagged host confirm it uses the vips processor and accepts untrusted uploads (else de-prioritize), and check internet exposure. 2) Contain: patch Active Storage to 7.2.3.2/8.0.5.1/8.1.3.1, upgrade libvips to ≥8.13, and set VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED / Vips.block_untrusted(true); apply WAF virtual patch where immediate upgrade isn't possible. 3) Hunt: retro-scan UC1/UC2/UC3 telemetry on every exposed host for prior exploitation before the patch window.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-66066"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d) | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, IsInternetFacing, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-66066"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, OSPlatform, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve="CVE-2026-66066" by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Vulnerabilities where Vulnerabilities.cve="CVE-2026-66066" by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity

ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-66066")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-66066")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Exposure hunt: hosts loading poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js (s2.adform.net) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender

Adform crypto-clipper C2 beacon to 84.32.102.230:7744 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js beacon: on page load the injected code issues an HTTP request to 84.32.102.230 on TCP 7744 carrying the victim page hostname/path. Any host in the fleet connecting to this IP:port is a browser that rendered the trojanized script. The IP:port pair is a hard IOC confirmed by multiple second sources. Rationale: 84.32.102.230:7744 is the exact C2 endpoint the injected code beacons to on page load, corroborated by BleepingComputer and Beaumont's DoublePulsar analysis. TCP 7744 is a non-standard port, so IP+port together is a near-zero-FP hard IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firm-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/ • https://www.it-connect.tech/adform-breach-ad-script-steals-cryptocurrency-for-at-least-a-week/
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-intel / SOC analyst deliberately curling the IOC to validate it
  • Vulnerability scanner or attack-surface tool probing 84.32.102.230
  • Security sandbox detonating a captured copy of the script
  • Honeypot / deception host intentionally reaching the C2
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","arc.exe") // keep only browser-originated beacons; drop analyst/scanner curl/python validation
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is a browser (chrome/edge/firefox) and pull the DeviceName/user; the connection means that endpoint rendered a page carrying poisoned trackpoint-async.js. 2) Contain: block 84.32.102.230 (all ports, esp. 7744) at egress/firewall, force-clear browser cache on affected hosts per Adform guidance, and warn the user to verify any crypto wallet address before sending funds. 3) Hunt: pivot on all internal hosts that loaded s2.adform.net during 2026-07-20..27 (see companion exposure UC) and review any crypto transactions initiated from affected endpoints in that window for swapped addresses.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "84.32.102.230" and RemotePort == 7744
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "84.32.102.230" and DestinationPort == 7744
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposure hunt: hosts loading poisoned Adform trackpoint-async.js (s2.adform.net) AIDelivery Medium
IR-scoping hunt for endpoints/users that fetched trackpoint-async.js from s2.adform.net during the compromise window (~2026-07-20 to 2026-07-27). Because the URL is legitimate, this is a hunting/exposure query to enumerate who received the poisoned resource, not a standalone alert. Pair with the C2 beacon UC to confirm actual execution. Rationale: trackpoint-async.js served from s2.adform.net is the exact poisoned resource named in the article and confirmed by BleepingComputer/DoublePulsar. Scoping to the 2026-07-20..27 window turns an otherwise-legit ad request into an exposure list for IR; low fidelity by design, so tiered as hunting. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/online-ad-firm-adforms-script-compromised-to-steal-cryptocurrency/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1189
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Adform tag loads on marketing/e-commerce sites your users browse (the URL is benign — expect high volume)
  • CDN/DNS-only telemetry (Falcon DnsRequest) cannot confirm the poisoned file version, only that the host resolved s2.adform.net
  • HTTPS proxy without TLS inspection sees only the domain, not the trackpoint-async.js path
  • Cached copies of the script served after Adform's fix still match the URL
Response runbook
1) Triage: treat the output as an exposure list, not confirmed compromise — cross-reference each host against the C2 beacon UC (84.32.102.230:7744) to find endpoints that actually executed the payload. 2) Contain: force browser cache clear on listed hosts (the poisoned file may persist in cache per Adform's advisory) and advise affected users to verify wallet addresses before any crypto transfer. 3) Hunt: for confirmed hosts, review clipboard-driven crypto payments and outbound wallet transactions during 2026-07-20..27 for address substitution, and check whether other Adform-hosted scripts on those pages also beaconed to 84.32.102.230.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp between (datetime(2026-07-20) .. datetime(2026-07-28))
| where RemoteUrl has "s2.adform.net"
| where RemoteUrl has "trackpoint-async.js" or RemoteUrl endswith "s2.adform.net"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl
| order by FirstSeen asc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated between (datetime(2026-07-20) .. datetime(2026-07-28))
| where Url has "trackpoint-async.js" and Url has "adform"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by FirstSeen asc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'

        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'

falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

Hijacked Hotel Wi-Fi Pushes Fake Updates to Deliver Surveillance Malware

The Hacker News
2026-08-01 16 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A fake browser update served over hijacked hotel Wi-Fi has been used to deliver CornFlake, a remote access trojan (RAT) that can capture webcam images, microphone audio, and keystrokes, Microsoft said in its latest report. CornFlake implant masquerade: svchost32.exe running from %APPDATA%\svchost32 AIInstallation High
Hunts the CornFlake RAT dropped by CaptiveCrunch, which copies itself to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe — a name/location masquerade of the legitimate System32 svchost.exe. Any process literally named svchost32.exe, or a svchost32.exe executing outside System32/SysWOW64, is article-specific and high-fidelity. Rationale: Anchored on the literal CornFlake artifact from the article: %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe. svchost32.exe is not a real Windows binary, so the name alone plus the non-System32 path is a near-unique signature. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0016/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wifi-pushes-fake.html
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom in-house tooling deliberately named svchost32.exe (rare, but exists in some legacy shops)
  • Security-vendor sandbox/emulation renaming samples during detonation
  • Admin-staged test binaries in a lab imaging share
Suppression filter
| where not (SHA256 in~ ("<known-good-internal-hash-if-any>"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull SHA256 and FolderPath — confirm the path is under \AppData\Roaming\svchost32\ and the file is unsigned; check first-seen time on the host. 2) Contain: isolate the device in Defender/EDR, kill the svchost32.exe process, and quarantine the binary (a watchdog restores persistence, so isolate before deleting). 3) Hunt: pivot on the SHA256 org-wide, then check for the svchost32 service ('Cloud Sync Service'), Run-key, scheduled task, and outbound connections to the CaptiveCrunch C2 IPs/domains.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "svchost32.exe" or FolderPath has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| where FolderPath !has @"\System32\" and FolderPath !has @"\SysWOW64\"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has @"\svchost32.exe"
| where NewProcessName !has @"\System32\" and NewProcessName !has @"\SysWOW64\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CornFlake persistence: svchost32 service 'Cloud Sync Service' + Run key + scheduled task AIInstallation High
Hunts the CornFlake persistence layer: a Windows service named svchost32 with display name 'Cloud Sync Service', plus a Registry Run key and scheduled task all pointing at %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe. A watchdog restores any removed mechanism, so the write itself is the signal. Rationale: Uses the exact service name (svchost32), display name ('Cloud Sync Service') and target binary path named in the article — a triad that legitimate software will not reproduce. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0016/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wifi-pushes-fake.html
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1543.003 T1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Services Endpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate cloud-sync product genuinely named 'Cloud Sync Service' (verify the ImagePath is NOT under \AppData\)
  • Admin creating a test service during troubleshooting
  • GPO/endpoint-mgmt agent writing Run keys during imaging
Suppression filter
| where ServiceFileName !has @"\Program Files\" and ServiceFileName !has @"\Program Files (x86)\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm ServiceFileName / Run value resolves to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe and the writing process is not a trusted installer. 2) Contain: isolate host, then remove ALL persistence (service, Run key, scheduled task) simultaneously because the CornFlake watchdog restores individually-deleted ones. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same service/Run value and correlate to prior svchost32.exe execution and C2 egress.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RegistryValueData has "svchost32" or RegistryValueData has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" or RegistryValueData has "Cloud Sync Service")
| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\Services\svchost32", "Cloud Sync Service")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 7045
| where ServiceName =~ "svchost32" or ServiceName has "Cloud Sync Service" or ServiceFileName has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType, ServiceType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ChocoShell token theft: non-broker process touching Token Broker .tbres cache AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the ChocoShell in-memory PowerShell stealer, which harvests M365/Entra access, refresh and WAM tokens from .tbres files in the Token Broker cache to enable browserless session replay. Legitimate .tbres access is only by Microsoft broker processes; any other process is anomalous. Rationale: The article names the exact ChocoShell target — .tbres files in the Token Broker cache holding M365/Entra/WAM tokens. Baselining that only the Microsoft broker family touches these files makes any other reader/copier high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0016/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wifi-pushes-fake.html
ATT&CKT1528 T1550.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint backup/DLP agents that index the user profile including \TokenBroker\Cache
  • AV/EDR full-disk scans reading .tbres files
  • Migration/profile-roaming tooling copying AppData
  • Developer diagnostics against WAM token cache
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "MsMpEng.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the accessing process and its parent — confirm it is not a backup/AV agent; check if it is powershell.exe/pwsh.exe or svchost32.exe. 2) Contain: isolate the host and, in Entra, revoke the user's refresh tokens/sessions (revokeSignInSessions) since stolen .tbres tokens enable browserless replay. 3) Hunt: review SigninLogs for non-interactive/token-based sign-ins from unfamiliar IPs for that user, and check for device-code sign-ins.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".tbres" or FolderPath has @"\Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache\"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("svchost.exe","TokenBroker.exe","Microsoft.AAD.BrokerPlugin.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe","backgroundTaskHost.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".tbres" or TargetFilePath has @"\Microsoft\TokenBroker\Cache\"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("svchost.exe","TokenBroker.exe","Microsoft.AAD.BrokerPlugin.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe","backgroundTaskHost.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, DvcAction, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CaptiveCrunch OAuth device code authentication phishing / approval AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts CaptiveCrunch landing pages (since July 16) that funnel guests into Microsoft's device code authentication flow, where entering the attacker-supplied code on the legitimate sign-in page grants the attacker an MFA-satisfied session. Surfaces successful device-code sign-ins for review against Conditional Access. Rationale: Directly targets the article's July-16 pivot to Microsoft's device code authentication flow. Successful device-code sign-ins are rare in most tenants, so listing them for CA review is the recommended article-aligned control. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0016/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wifi-pushes-fake.html
ATT&CKT1528 T1621
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate device-code use on input-constrained devices (smart TVs, conference room / Teams Rooms, IoT)
  • PowerShell/CLI tooling (Az/Graph) using device-code auth
  • Onboarding of shared kiosk devices
  • Developers testing device-code apps
Suppression filter
| where AppDisplayName !in ("Microsoft Teams Rooms", "Microsoft Authentication Broker") and ClientAppUsed != "Mobile Apps and Desktop clients"
Response runbook
1) Triage: correlate the sign-in IP/UA and the user's normal location — device-code sign-ins from hospitality/public IPs or foreign geos are suspicious. 2) Contain: revoke sessions/refresh tokens for the user and enable a Conditional Access policy blocking device-code flow where not required. 3) Hunt: pivot the source IP across SigninLogs/AADNonInteractive for other victims and check subsequent mailbox/OneDrive access from the same session.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "deviceCode"
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, ApplicationId, IPAddress, Country, City, ResourceDisplayName, ConditionalAccessStatus, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent
| order by Timestamp desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "Device Code" or AuthenticationProcessingDetails has "deviceCode"
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, AppId, IPAddress, tostring(LocationDetails), ResourceDisplayName, ConditionalAccessStatus, ClientAppUsed, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CaptiveCrunch C2: callbacks to CornFlake IPs and Microsoft-impersonating domains AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint/network egress to the CaptiveCrunch infrastructure — the four CornFlake C2 IPs and the five Microsoft-impersonating domains (m365-owa.com, owa-ms365.com, ms365-device.com, ms365-live.com, deltaode.com). Any connection or DNS resolution to these indicators is a direct campaign hit. Rationale: Pure IOC match on the pre-extracted CornFlake C2 IPs and the five Microsoft-impersonating domains documented by both Microsoft and ReliaQuest. Sentinel query rewritten to use DestinationIP (CommonSecurityLog) and Name/ServerIPAddress (DnsEvents) instead of the invalid IPAddresses column. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0016/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wifi-pushes-fake.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel sandbox or research host deliberately resolving the IOCs
  • Security scanner/proxy pre-fetching flagged URLs
  • Shared hosting IP later re-used by a benign service (validate IP freshness before alerting)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — a hit from svchost32.exe or powershell.exe is a confirmed CornFlake/ChocoShell C2 beacon. 2) Contain: block the IPs/domains at the proxy/firewall and isolate the source host. 3) Hunt: expand the time window on the source IP for additional victims, and correlate to prior fake-update execution and .tbres/token theft on the same device.

ClickFix fake update: browser/Run-dialog spawns interpreter fetching CaptiveCrunch infra AIDelivery High
Hunts the CaptiveCrunch ClickFix delivery, where a fake browser/OS update page instructs the victim to open a terminal and run an attacker-supplied command. Detects an interpreter (PowerShell/cmd/mshta/curl) spawned by a browser or explorer.exe whose command line references the campaign's C2 domains, IPs, or the svchost32 payload. Rationale: Combines the ClickFix TTP (browser/Run-dialog spawning an interpreter) with a mandatory campaign-infra command-line anchor (C2 domains/IPs or svchost32), which keeps it distinct from generic phishing-click rules and produces very low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0016/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wifi-pushes-fake.html
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher reproducing the ClickFix chain in a lab
  • Red-team engagement replaying the exact IOCs
  • IT distributing a genuine script that happens to reference one of these strings (unlikely given the impersonation domains)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--headless" and DeviceName !startswith "LAB-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full ProcessCommandLine/InitiatingProcessCommandLine — capture the download URL and any staged path (%APPDATA%\svchost32). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the interpreter and any child svchost32.exe, and block the referenced domains/IPs. 3) Hunt: check whether the payload persisted (service/Run key), whether .tbres tokens were touched, and whether the user later completed a device-code sign-in.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com","ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","deltaode.com","svchost32","31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150","38.146.28.75","89.124.79.98")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("explorer.exe","chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe","curl.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("m365-owa.com","owa-ms365.com","ms365-device.com","ms365-live.com","deltaode.com","svchost32","31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150","38.146.28.75","89.124.79.98")

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Captive-portal DNS hijack: NCSI connectivity check resolving to CaptiveCrunch IPs AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the CaptiveCrunch initial-access technique where a hijacked captive-portal gateway (also the assigned DNS resolver) forges DNS answers to redirect a device's automatic connectivity check to a fake update page. Detects Windows NCSI/connectivity-check hostnames resolving to, or connecting to, the known CaptiveCrunch C2 IPs. Rationale: Models the article's described mechanism — captive-portal gateway forging DNS to redirect the automatic connectivity check. Pairing the Windows NCSI hostnames (msftconnecttest.com / msftncsi.com) with a resolved/connected IP inside the known CaptiveCrunch C2 set makes DNS-forgery detectable and low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G0016/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wifi-pushes-fake.html
ATT&CKT1557 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign service later re-hosted on one of these IPs (validate IOC freshness)
  • Captive-portal vendor intentionally answering NCSI to trigger the login splash (this is legitimate captive-portal behavior — verify the IP is attacker-owned, not the venue gateway)
  • Corporate proxy rewriting NCSI checks
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the device was on a hospitality/public network and that the NCSI hostname resolved to an attacker IP rather than a Microsoft-owned range. 2) Contain: instruct the user to disconnect from the venue Wi-Fi and switch to the always-on full-tunnel VPN; isolate if a payload followed. 3) Hunt: on the same device, look for a subsequent fake-update ClickFix execution, svchost32.exe drop, and C2 egress; advise travelers to reject captive-portal update/cert/tool offers.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("msftconnecttest.com","msftncsi.com")
| where RemoteIP in ("31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150","38.146.28.75","89.124.79.98")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationHostName has_any ("msftconnecttest.com","msftncsi.com") or RequestURL has_any ("msftconnecttest.com","msftncsi.com")
| where DestinationIP in ("31.57.243.154","104.194.159.150","38.146.28.75","89.124.79.98")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DestinationIP, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

references:

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

// Article-specific bespoke detection — Hijacked Hotel Wi-Fi Pushes Fake Updates to Deliver Surveillance Malware
// Hunts the actual binaries / paths / commandline fragments named
// in the article instead of a generic technique-class template.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName in~ ("svchost32.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("%APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName,
          FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (FolderPath has_any ("%APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe") or FileName in~ ("svchost32.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath,
          FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
