ApostropheCMS $pullAll __proto__ prototype-pollution PATCH (CVE-2026-53609) AIExploitation High
Hunts the exploit request itself: a PATCH to an ApostropheCMS piece-type REST endpoint whose body carries prototype-pollution tokens ($pullAll with __proto__/constructor/prototype, typically targeting publicApiProjection). This is the single request that poisons Object.prototype and bypasses authorization process-wide. Requires WAF/proxy telemetry that inspects or logs the request body. Rationale: Uses the article's exact PoC tokens ($pullAll, __proto__, publicApiProjection) and the /api/v1/@apostrophecms/ REST path plus PATCH method — the precise shape of the poisoning request. Body-capture required; empty for Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudTrail since none carry inbound HTTP to a Node CMS. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/ • https://www.thehackerwire.com/apostrophecms-critical-prototype-pollution-leads-to-auth-bypass/ • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-53609-cwe-1321-improperly-controlled-modi-874d30d1
ATT&CKT1190 T1548
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (nuclei/Burp/Nessus) firing generic prototype-pollution payloads at the endpoint
  • Authorized pentest or the security team re-running the public PoC in staging
  • WAF already blocking the request (DeviceAction=block) — attempted, not successful, exploitation
  • Bug-bounty researcher probing a public site
Suppression filter
| where DeviceAction != "block" and DeviceAction != "Blocked"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full PATCH body for the SourceIP and confirm $pullAll + __proto__/constructor targeting publicApiProjection; check DeviceAction to see if the WAF blocked or passed it; identify the editor account/token that authenticated the PATCH. 2) Contain: if passed, restart the affected Node.js process immediately (pollution persists in-memory until restart), rotate the editor's credentials/session token, block the source IP at the WAF, and upgrade Apostrophe to 4.31.0. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC 'authorization-bypass' to see whether unauthenticated 200s followed on /api/v1/@apostrophecms/* and enumerate what data was exposed.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "PATCH"
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/"
| where RequestURL has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll","constructor","publicApiProjection")
    or RequestContext has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll","publicApiProjection")
    or Message has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll","publicApiProjection")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestContext, Message, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ApostropheCMS auth bypass: unauthenticated endpoint flips notfound(404)→200 (CVE-2026-53609) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the impact of successful prototype pollution: a source IP that previously received notfound/401/403 on protected piece-type endpoints (/user, /global) begins receiving HTTP 200 without authenticating. In the PoC the protected endpoint returns the 'notfound' error (HTTP 404) pre-exploit and a valid paginated 200 post-exploit. Rationale: Grounded in the PoC's before/after: Step 1 returns the 'notfound' error (HTTP 404) unauthenticated, Step 4 returns 200 with results and no credentials. Baselining a source that transitions deny→allow on /user and /global captures the process-wide bypass without needing body capture. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/ • https://dailycve.com/apostrophecms-server-side-prototype-pollution-leading-to-authorization-bypass-cve-2026-53609-critical-dc-aug2026-1218/
ATT&CKT1548 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint legitimately configured with publicApiProjection so anonymous 200s are expected (real Apostrophe feature)
  • Shared NAT/proxy egress IP where one client 404s and a genuinely authenticated client 200s
  • App restart / deploy causing status-code shifts for the same IP
  • Uptime monitor or crawler hitting the endpoints repeatedly
Suppression filter
| where not (CsUriStem == "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global")   // remove if /global is intentionally public; keep /user which is never public
Response runbook
1) Triage: for the flagged CIp, order events by time and confirm 404/401/403 precede the 200 with no successful /api/v1/@apostrophecms/login/login in between; verify the endpoint is NOT intentionally public (publicApiProjection). 2) Contain: restart the Node.js process to clear the polluted Object.prototype, upgrade to Apostrophe 4.31.0, and revoke sessions; block the offending IP. 3) Hunt: correlate with the $pullAll PATCH UC to find the originating poison request and the editor account, and quantify which piece-type records were exfiltrated during the 200 window.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CsUriStem in ("/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user","/api/v1/@apostrophecms/global")
| summarize denies = countif(ScStatus in (401,403,404)), allows = countif(ScStatus == 200), firstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), lastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by CIp, CsUriStem
| where denies >= 3 and allows >= 1   // 404(notfound)/401/403 history that flips to 200 = post-poison access
| order by allows desc

ApostropheCMS exploit chain: $pullAll PATCH then unauth GET 200 within 30s (CVE-2026-53609) AIExploitation High
Correlates the two-step exploit: a PATCH to /api/v1/@apostrophecms/* from a source IP followed within 30 seconds by a successful (200) GET to /user or /global from the same IP that lands after the poisoning. Sequencing the mutation and the resulting bypass sharply raises confidence over either signal alone. Rationale: Maps directly to the article's PoC ordering (Step 3 PATCH poison → Step 4 unauthenticated 200 on /user). The 30s same-source window ties the mutation to the resulting bypass and eliminates lone editor PATCHes and lone public reads. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/apostrophe/CVE-2026-53609/
ATT&CKT1190 T1548
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Editor saves a doc (PATCH) then immediately browses a legitimately public piece from the same IP
  • Synthetic monitoring that PATCHes and GETs in sequence
  • Shared egress IP where an editor's PATCH coincides with another user's public 200
  • CI/CD smoke tests exercising the REST API
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve the PatchUri body — confirm $pullAll/__proto__ tokens; if body isn't logged, treat the temporal PATCH→200 pairing as high-suspicion and check whether the GET's 200 is anomalous for an unauthenticated caller. 2) Contain: restart the Node process to clear pollution, upgrade to 4.31.0, rotate the editor credential behind the PATCH, and block the source IP. 3) Hunt: sweep all /api/v1/@apostrophecms/* endpoints for further unauthenticated 200s from that IP and any other IPs benefiting from the same poisoned process before restart.

Atomic Arch AUR loader/stealer known-bad file & process hashes AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution or on-disk presence of the July 2026 AUR (openconnect-sso) two-stage loader and Rust infostealer by their published SHA256/MD5 hashes. Article-specific: these hashes belong to the IFIN-analyzed Atomic Arch campaign redistributed through hijacked AUR package adoptions. Rationale: Uses the four campaign SHA256 hashes plus the MD5 pre-extracted from the article; SHA256 6144d433... is independently confirmed as the Rust stealer binary by The Hacker News and GuardSix, so hash-based matching is high-fidelity with near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse • https://discourse.ifin.network/t/new-aur-attack-prompts-adoption-lock/698

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the sample in an authorized sandbox that reports to production EDR
  • Threat-intel/VirusTotal retrohunt downloads of the sample onto a research host
  • Incident-response tooling copying the artifact for evidence collection
  • Backup/AV quarantine re-scanning a previously captured copy
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("clamscan","freshclam","vt","virustotal") and FolderPath !has "/quarantine/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is Arch/Arch-based and whether any AUR package (openconnect-sso, boringssl-git, icloudpd, windscribe-cli-v2-bin, stirling-pdf-desktop-bin, pgadmin4-server) was recently installed/updated via makepkg. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the matching PID, and treat all local secrets (SSH keys, browser creds, cloud/dev/AI tokens) as compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process, systemd units with Restart=always, and cron entries; rotate SSH keys and check known_hosts targets for lateral spread.

Tor client masquerading as dbus-daemon making external network connections AICommand & Control High
Hunts the Atomic Arch first-stage behaviour of launching a Tor client renamed to 'dbus-daemon' to reach an .onion C2. A legitimate dbus-daemon is a local IPC bus and never initiates public/internet egress, so any outbound public connection from a dbus-daemon process is high-fidelity. Rationale: Article states the loader 'downloads and launches a Tor client disguised as dbus-daemon' to reach an .onion server; corroborated by GuardSix noting C2 via a Tor onion service. dbus-daemon making public egress (Defender/Falcon) or running outside /usr/bin (Sentinel/Datadog/Sigma) is essentially never legitimate. Cross-checked against: • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1036.005 T1573.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom-built dbus deployed to a non-standard prefix (/usr/local/bin) on developer boxes — path variant only
  • D-Bus remote/TCP transport intentionally configured in a container or CI runner
  • Chaos/network-testing tooling renamed to system binaries during red-team exercises
  • Flatpak/snap sandboxes shipping their own dbus-daemon under /app or /snap paths
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !in~ ("/usr/bin","/usr/local/bin") or RemotePort in (9001, 9030, 9050, 443)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full path, hash, and command line of the dbus-daemon process; a real one lives at /usr/bin/dbus-daemon and only talks to unix sockets — confirm the destination IP/port and whether it looks like a Tor guard node (443/9001). 2) Contain: isolate the host and kill the process; block the destination IP at egress. 3) Hunt: locate the parent AUR build (makepkg), the second-stage stealer under /var/lib or ~/.config, and any systemd/cron persistence; rotate all secrets on the host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "dbus-daemon"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 10), RemoteIPs = make_set(RemoteIP, 25) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "dbus-daemon"
| where TargetProcessName !has "/usr/bin/dbus-daemon"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Non-package-manager process writing systemd unit or cron persistence (Atomic Arch) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the loader's persistence step: writing a systemd service (Restart=always) to /etc/systemd/system or ~/.config/systemd/user, plus cron jobs, from a process that is NOT a package manager or systemctl. Article-specific to the AUR loader installing systemd services and cron jobs after anti-analysis checks. Rationale: Article states the loader 'installs systemd services and cron jobs to ensure persistence'; StepSecurity/GuardSix confirm a Restart=always unit dropped to /etc/systemd/system (root) or ~/.config/systemd/user (user). Keying on non-package-manager writers to these exact paths captures the malicious writer while excluding legit installs to /usr/lib/systemd/system. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/400-aur-packages-hijacked-atomic-arch-campaign • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse
ATT&CKT1543.002 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin hand-authoring a unit with a text editor (vim/nano) or writing crontab via a script
  • Configuration management (Ansible/Chef/Puppet/Salt) deploying systemd units or cron jobs
  • Developer enabling a user service under ~/.config/systemd/user for a legitimate app
  • Container build steps or dotfile-management tools writing unit files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","ansible-playbook","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion","vim","nano","vi","tee") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","puppet","chef","salt"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the dropped unit/cron file — malicious ones point ExecStart at a binary under /var/lib, ~/.config, /tmp or /dev/shm and use Restart=always; benign ones point at packaged binaries in /usr/bin. 2) Contain: disable/remove the unit or cron entry, kill the referenced binary, and isolate the host if the target is a non-package path. 3) Hunt: pivot to the writing process's ancestry (makepkg build?), check for the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process and stealer artifacts, and rotate host secrets.

| where FileName endswith ".service" or FolderPath has "cron"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("systemctl","systemd","pacman","dpkg","apt","apt-get","rpm","dnf","yum","install","crontab")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

SSH worm: persistence-path binary spawning ssh/scp for self-propagation AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Atomic Arch stealer's SSH worm capability — a binary running from a malware persistence directory (/var/lib, ~/.config, /tmp, /dev/shm) spawning ssh/scp/sftp/rsync to copy and execute itself on other hosts using stolen SSH keys. Distinguishes malware-driven lateral movement from interactive/administrative SSH. Rationale: Article states the stealer 'can spread laterally by using stolen SSH keys to copy and execute itself on other systems'; corroborated by StepSecurity/HackerNews noting SSH-key and known_hosts theft. Anchoring on ssh/scp spawned by a parent living in the confirmed persistence directories (/var/lib for root, ~/.config for user) targets the worm rather than routine admin SSH. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/400-aur-packages-hijacked-atomic-arch-campaign
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom deployment/orchestration scripts installed under /var/lib or a user's ~/.config wrapper that call scp/rsync
  • CI/CD runner or backup agent staged in /tmp or /var/lib performing rsync-over-ssh
  • Developer helper tools in ~/.config invoking git-over-ssh (partly excluded via git filter)
  • Config-management agents copying files to fleet hosts over ssh
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ansible","rsnapshot","borg","restic","rclone") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gitlab-runner","buildkite-agent","jenkins")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the parent binary's path, hash, and the ssh/scp command line — note the destination host/user and whether a copy of the parent binary is being transferred. 2) Contain: isolate the source host, kill the process, and pre-emptively isolate the destination host(s) named in the command line; revoke/rotate the SSH keys used. 3) Hunt: on each destination host, hunt for the same persistence (systemd Restart=always, cron), the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process, and the campaign hashes; expand outward via known_hosts entries.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("ssh","scp","sftp","rsync")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/var/lib/","/tmp/","/.config/","/dev/shm/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git","ansible","ansible-playbook","bash","sh","zsh","fish","rsync","ssh","code")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/ssh","/scp","/sftp","/rsync")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/var/lib/","/tmp/","/.config/","/dev/shm/")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("/git","/ansible","/bash","/sh","/zsh","/fish","/rsync","/ssh"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

      - '/scp'
      - '/sftp'
      - '/rsync'
    ParentImage|contains:
      - '/var/lib/'
      - '/tmp/'
      - '/.config/'
      - '/dev/shm/'
  filter:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/git'
      - '/ansible'
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
      - '/zsh'
      - '/fish'
  condition: selection and not filter
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(scp OR rsync OR sftp) @process.command_line:(*/var/lib/* OR */dev/shm/* OR */.config/*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\/(ssh|scp|sftp|rsync)$/i
| ParentImageFileName=/(\/var\/lib\/|\/tmp\/|\/\.config\/|\/dev\/shm\/)/i
| NOT ParentBaseFileName=/(git|ansible|bash|sh|zsh|fish|rsync|ssh)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentImageFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("ssh","scp","sftp","rsync")) (Processes.parent_process_path IN ("*/var/lib/*","*/tmp/*","*/.config/*","*/dev/shm/*")) NOT (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("git","ansible","bash","sh","zsh","fish","rsync","ssh")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process_path Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or SHA1 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or MD5 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or SHA1 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or MD5 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised Adform trackpoint-async.js clipper script by SHA256 on endpoint
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Online ad firm Adform’s script compromised to steal cryptocurrency
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] C2 beacon to Adform clipper attacker server 84.32.102.230:7744 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
C2 beacon to Adform clipper attacker server 84.32.102.230:7744 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the attacker-controlled server (84.32.102.230, port 7744) that the trojanized Adform scripts beaconed to, exfiltrating victim IP, referring website and URL path. Any host reaching this IP indicates a browser that loaded the compromised trackpoint-async.js during the July 2026 supply-chain window. Rationale: 84.32.102.230:7744 is the attacker-controlled C2 confirmed in both Beaumont's DoublePulsar analysis and BleepingComputer; it is not owned by Adform and has no benign use, making any connection a high-fidelity indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.it-connect.tech/adform-breach-ad-script-steals-cryptocurrency-for-at-least-a-week/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1195.002 T1115
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or malware sandbox intentionally detonating the IOC
  • Threat-intel scanner/crawler validating the C2 from an internal host
  • IP later reassigned to a benign shared-hosting tenant (verify port 7744 and date window July 2026)
  • Corporate VPN/proxy egress IP coincidentally matching (unlikely - it's a /32 attacker host)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host, user and initiating process for the connection; confirm it is a browser (chrome.exe/msedge.exe/firefox.exe) and whether the timestamp falls in the 26-27 July 2026 window. 2) Contain: block 84.32.102.230 at firewall/proxy, and if repeated beaconing is seen, isolate the host and force browser cache/cookie clearing per Adform's guidance. 3) Hunt: pivot to all other hosts that touched this IP, warn affected users to re-verify any crypto wallet addresses they copied/pasted recently, and check for the malicious script hash (see companion UC).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "84.32.102.230"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "84.32.102.230"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised Adform trackpoint-async.js clipper script by SHA256 on endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Retro-hunts the fleet for the exact malicious trojanized Adform tracking library (SHA256 02ff86c7...) landing on disk, typically as a browser cache artifact, to scope which endpoints downloaded the crypto-clipper during the supply-chain window. VirusTotal flagged this file clean across all engines, so hash-based hunting is required rather than AV signal. Rationale: SHA256 02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55 is the pre-extracted hash of the injected library; because VirusTotal shows zero detections, an exact-hash file hunt is the only reliable way to scope endpoint exposure. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.it-connect.tech/adform-breach-ad-script-steals-cryptocurrency-for-at-least-a-week/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1115 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A DFIR analyst intentionally saving the sample to an endpoint for analysis
  • A copy of the sample pulled from Beaumont's Pastebin/Archive.org for internal review
  • Malware-repo or IOC-feed clone stored on a workstation
  • SHA256 collision (cryptographically negligible - treat any exact match as true positive)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path (browser cache dir vs a saved copy) and the FileOriginUrl/downloading process to distinguish a real infection from analyst handling. 2) Contain: on genuine infections, clear the affected browser's cache/cookies as Adform advises, block 84.32.102.230, and advise the user to re-check any crypto addresses copied on 26-27 July 2026. 3) Hunt: correlate matching hosts against the C2-beacon UC, and search proxy logs for retrievals of trackpoint-async.js from s2.adform.net/a1.adform.net/ai1.adform.net during the window to build the full impacted-user list.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 == "02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 == "02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01

description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or SHA1 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or MD5 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or SHA1 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or MD5 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware delivery and credential theft

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-31 17 use cases 15 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Storm-2945, a sub-cluster of the Russian threat actor Midnight Blizzard, has been observed compromising the sign-in portals of hospitality-related organizations such as hotels since May 2026 in order to deliver malware to travelers and steal credentials in an operation we call CaptiveCrunch. The post CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware delivery and credential theft appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Endpoint connections to Storm-2945 CaptiveCrunch AiTM doppelganger infrastructure · [LLM] CornFlake C2 egress from masqueraded svchost32.exe in AppData · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Entra ID sign-in or session from Storm-2945 AiTM device-code phishing infrastructure · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
CornFlake RAT persistence via svchost32.exe masquerade in %APPDATA% AIInstallation High
Hunts Storm-2945's CornFlake implant, which copies itself to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe and registers as a Windows service 'svchost32' (display name 'Cloud Sync Service') to masquerade as the legitimate System32 svchost.exe. Legitimate svchost.exe only ever runs from %SystemRoot%\System32, so any svchost32.exe under a user profile path is malicious by construction. Rationale: Anchored on the exact drop path %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe and service name 'svchost32'/'Cloud Sync Service' from the article; corroborated by ReliaQuest and The Hacker News. A binary named svchost32.exe outside System32 has no legitimate use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wi-fi-pushes-fake.html • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1036.005 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A niche third-party app that legitimately ships a file literally named svchost32.exe in AppData (extremely rare; none known)
  • Security researcher / IR analyst detonating the CornFlake sample in a sandbox on a monitored host
  • EDR sample-detonation or red-team emulation of this exact campaign
  • Backup/restore of an already-infected profile re-writing the path
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the SHA256 of svchost32.exe and confirm the parent process and the '\svchost32\svchost32.exe' path is under a user profile (never System32). Check for a service named svchost32 with display 'Cloud Sync Service'. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, stop and delete the svchost32 service, remove the Run key and scheduled task pointing at the binary, and force-revoke the user's Entra sessions/tokens (traveler likely token-compromised). 3) HUNT: Sweep for the same path/service org-wide, and pivot to DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound connections from svchost32.exe and to the doppelganger M365 domains/IOC IPs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" or FileName =~ "svchost32.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
union
(SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where EventID == 4688 | where NewProcessName endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Evidence=NewProcessName, Detail=CommandLine, Actor=SubjectUserName),
(SecurityEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where EventID == 4697 | where ServiceName =~ "svchost32" or ServiceFileName endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe" | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Evidence=ServiceName, Detail=ServiceFileName, Actor=SubjectUserName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Endpoint connections to Storm-2945 CaptiveCrunch AiTM doppelganger infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network connections and DNS lookups to the Storm-2945 doppelganger domains that mimic Microsoft 365 services (ms365-device.com, ms365-live.com, m365-owa.com, owa-ms365.com) and the campaign's actor-controlled IP infrastructure used for adversary-in-the-middle device-code phishing and M365 token theft. These are hard IOCs — any hit indicates a traveler routed through the CaptiveCrunch AiTM proxy. Rationale: Uses the article's exact doppelganger domain list and pre-extracted actor IP set (Block 2), cross-checked against ReliaQuest's write-up of the same infrastructure. These are unique lookalike domains with zero legitimate business use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://securityaffairs.com/196441/apt/russian-hackers-hijack-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-tokens.html
ATT&CKT1557 T1539 T1566.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security tool / TI feed pre-fetching or sinkholing these IOC domains for analysis
  • Analyst manually browsing to the domain during investigation from a corporate host
  • Passive DNS / URL-scanning services running from the monitored range
  • IP reuse after takedown where the IP is reassigned to a benign host (verify domain hit alongside IP)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify which user/device connected and whether the connection carried an M365 auth flow (browser process, Referer to login.microsoftonline.com). Confirm the device was on untrusted Wi-Fi (hotel/conference). 2) CONTAIN: Revoke the user's Entra refresh tokens and sign-in sessions immediately, require re-registration of MFA, and block the domains/IPs at proxy and firewall. 3) HUNT: Check Entra sign-in logs for the same user authenticating from the actor IPs and for any new device registration; sweep the endpoint for CornFlake (svchost32.exe) delivered on the same session.

let target_ips = dynamic(["31.57.243.154","38.146.28.75","38.146.28.132","104.194.159.150","107.189.26.194","213.145.86.112"]);

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any(target_domains) or RemoteIP in (target_ips)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc

(DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has_any (target_domains) | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, Result)

Entra ID sign-in or session from Storm-2945 AiTM device-code phishing infrastructure AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects successful Entra ID authentications originating from Storm-2945's actor-controlled IP infrastructure, the tail end of the CaptiveCrunch device-code AiTM flow where a phished traveler's device code authenticates the attacker's session. Anchors on the campaign's confirmed IP set as the sign-in source. Rationale: Anchors on the article's actor IP set as the authentication source — a successful M365 sign-in from CaptiveCrunch infrastructure is a direct token-theft indicator; Volexity independently documents the same device-code AiTM technique for this actor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://www.volexity.com/blog/2025/02/13/multiple-russian-threat-actors-targeting-microsoft-device-code-authentication/ • https://phishingtackle.com/blog/russian-hackers-use-microsoft-device-code-phishing-in-targeted-attacks
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1528 T1098.005
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An IOC IP later reassigned by its hosting provider to a benign VPN/proxy a legitimate user transits
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance replaying sign-in test traffic
  • Corporate egress NAT coincidentally sharing a subnet with a taken-down IOC (verify exact /32)
  • Analyst reproducing the auth flow from an actor IP in a lab tenant
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the sign-in succeeded (ErrorCode/ResultType 0) and identify the app (Graph, OWA) and whether a new device was registered in the same window. 2) CONTAIN: Revoke all refresh tokens for the account, disable the account or force password reset + MFA re-enrollment, and remove any attacker-registered device from Entra. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the account to Graph/EWS mail-access and any OAuth app consent grants; check the user's endpoint for CornFlake and correlate to the doppelganger-domain connections from UC2.

AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where IPAddress in (target_ips)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, ApplicationId, IPAddress, Country, City, ClientAppUsed, DeviceTrustType, ConditionalAccessStatus, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc

(SigninLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where IPAddress in (target_ips) | where ResultType == 0 | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName, IPAddress, Location, ClientAppUsed, RiskLevelDuringSignIn),
(AuditLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where OperationName has "device" and Category =~ "Device" | extend Actor=tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), ActorIp=tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress) | where ActorIp in (target_ips) | project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Actor, ActorIp, Result)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ClickFix execution reaching CaptiveCrunch infrastructure or dropping svchost32 AIDelivery High
Detects the CaptiveCrunch ClickFix chain where a user is socially engineered (fake browser/OS update) into running a script interpreter whose command line reaches Storm-2945's doppelganger domains/IOC IPs or references the CornFlake drop path svchost32. Anchors the generic ClickFix pattern to this campaign's concrete IOCs to avoid template noise. Rationale: Pairs the ClickFix execution primitive (interpreter launch) with the campaign's hard IOCs (doppelganger domains, actor IPs, svchost32 drop path) so it fires only on this campaign, not on generic scripting — combination is high-fidelity per the article's ClickFix delivery description. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/hijacked-hotel-wi-fi-pushes-fake.html
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1059.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin script that legitimately references a host named 'svchost32' (rare; verify path context)
  • Security testing/red-team emulating the ClickFix chain in a lab
  • Threat-hunting query copy-pasted into a console leaving IOC strings in a shell history/command line
  • Sinkhole or research tooling curling the IOC domains for analysis
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Read the full command line — confirm which IOC it hit (domain download vs svchost32 reference) and the parent process (explorer.exe/browser indicates ClickFix paste). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the interpreter and any child svchost32.exe, and revoke the user's Entra tokens (traveler credential exposure). 3) HUNT: Pivot to DeviceFileEvents for the svchost32 drop and DeviceNetworkEvents for follow-on C2 to the IOC IPs; sweep other travelers for the same ClickFix command shape.

CornFlake C2 egress from masqueraded svchost32.exe in AppData AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound network connections initiated by the CornFlake implant running as svchost32.exe from a user AppData path. The legitimate svchost.exe lives only in System32 and its network activity is service-mediated, so public-internet egress from a profile-resident svchost32.exe is CornFlake C2 / data exfiltration beaconing. Rationale: Anchors on the CornFlake implant image/path (svchost32.exe under AppData, from the article) making outbound public connections — behaviorally impossible for the real System32 svchost.exe, so any hit is CornFlake beaconing. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/31/captivecrunch-midnight-blizzard-targets-travelers-worldwide-for-malware-delivery-and-credential-theft/ • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573 T1036.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox detonation of the CornFlake sample generating C2 traffic on a monitored host
  • Red-team emulation using a binary named svchost32.exe
  • A misconfigured third-party tool coincidentally named svchost32.exe (none known)
  • EDR telemetry replay/testing environments
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm InitiatingProcessFolderPath is a user AppData path and capture the RemoteIP/RemoteUrl destinations (correlate to the campaign IOC IPs). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, terminate svchost32.exe, remove its service/Run key/scheduled task persistence, and block the C2 destinations. 3) HUNT: Retrieve collected-data artifacts (keylogger/screenshot/audio files), revoke the traveler's Entra tokens, and sweep the fleet for the same process-to-public-IP pattern and the svchost32 drop path.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost32.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.

// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost32.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ReportId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] NocoBase anonymous signup then immediate myInAppChannels access (CVE-2026-52887 pre-exploit)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] NocoBase CVE-2026-52887 SQLi in /api/myInAppChannels:list filter[latestMsgReceiveTimestamp][$lt] · [LLM] PostgreSQL backend spawning shell/LOLBin (COPY ... TO PROGRAM RCE, CVE-2026-52887)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-52887: NocoBase: SQL injection in /api/myInAppChannel
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
NocoBase CVE-2026-52887 SQLi in /api/myInAppChannels:list filter[latestMsgReceiveTimestamp][$lt] AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact injection vector: a request to the myInAppChannels:list resource whose filter carries the latestMsgReceiveTimestamp[$lt] parameter loaded with PostgreSQL SQLi primitives (PG_SLEEP, stacked COPY ... TO PROGRAM, CASE WHEN oracles). The legit value of $lt is an epoch integer, so any SQL keyword in this parameter is high-fidelity exploitation of CVE-2026-52887. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable resource string 'myInAppChannels', the injectable parameter 'latestMsgReceiveTimestamp', and the article's live-verified payload tokens PG_SLEEP / COPY ... TO PROGRAM / CASE WHEN. A legit $lt is an integer epoch, so any SQL keyword in this param is exploitation, not noise. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message/CVE-2026-52887/ • https://github.com/nocobase/nocobase/pull/9001
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentest / sqlmap scan against the NocoBase instance (article notes sqlmap 1.10.3 reproduces this)
  • Vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Nuclei) firing the CVE-2026-52887 template
  • Security researcher validating the patch on a staging host
  • WAF in monitor-only mode logging blocked-but-recorded attempts
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("10.0.0.0")  // add authorized scanner / pentest source IPs here
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request URL and source IP; confirm the $lt value contains SQL rather than a bare integer, and check the response status/latency (a ~5s delay = successful PG_SLEEP oracle). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/proxy, and if the request succeeded, treat the NocoBase DB container as compromised — rotate the super-admin credential and disable allowSignUp. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP for prior /api/auth:signUp and /api/auth:signIn calls, and check the Postgres host for postgres-spawned shell processes (UC3).
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "myInAppChannels"
| where Url has "latestMsgReceiveTimestamp"
| where Url has_any ("pg_sleep","PG_SLEEP","TO PROGRAM","TO%20PROGRAM","COPY","CASE WHEN","CASE%20WHEN","UNION","pg_read_file")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DvcHostname, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

NocoBase anonymous signup then immediate myInAppChannels access (CVE-2026-52887 pre-exploit) AIDelivery Medium
Correlates a successful anonymous account creation via /api/auth:signUp (enabled by the default allowSignUp:true) with a request to the vulnerable /api/myInAppChannels:list resource from the same source IP within minutes. This is the article's stated exploitation prerequisite: sign up, sign in, then hit the loggedIn-ACL endpoint. Rationale: Chains the two article-named endpoints — /api/auth:signUp (default allowSignUp:true) and the vulnerable /api/myInAppChannels:list — on a shared source IP inside a 10-minute window, matching the documented signup→signin→exploit flow. Same-IP correlation strips ordinary user browsing. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message/CVE-2026-52887/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate new-user onboarding where the account genuinely opens the in-app notifications panel
  • QA/automation account provisioning against a test instance
  • Load-testing or synthetic monitoring that signs up then exercises the API
  • Shared corporate egress IP where one user signs up and another (behind same NAT) opens notifications
Suppression filter
| where DvcHostname !has "staging" and DvcHostname !has "test"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the myInAppChannels request query for SQLi tokens (UC1) — signup+access alone is suspicious, signup+injection is confirmed exploitation. 2) Contain: if the follow-on request carries injection, block the IP and disable auth-basic allowSignUp (POST-signup should require admin approval). 3) Hunt: enumerate all accounts created via /api/auth:signUp in the window and review their subsequent API activity for data exfil (COPY reads of the users table).
let Signups = ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "auth:signUp" or Url has "auth%3AsignUp"
| where tostring(HttpStatusCode) in ("200","201")
| project SignupTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "myInAppChannels"
| join kind=inner Signups on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated between (SignupTime .. SignupTime + 10m)
| project SignupTime, AccessTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, Url
| order by AccessTime desc

PostgreSQL backend spawning shell/LOLBin (COPY ... TO PROGRAM RCE, CVE-2026-52887) AIExploitation High
Detects the RCE tail of CVE-2026-52887: the PostgreSQL backend process (running as uid=999 postgres in the DB container) spawning a shell or command binary via COPY ... TO PROGRAM. A postgres process should never fork sh/bash/id/curl, so this parent→child pair is a near-certain indicator of stacked-statement SQLi execution. Rationale: Anchored on the article's confirmed RCE mechanics: COPY ... TO PROGRAM runs shell as uid=999(postgres). A postgres parent forking sh/bash/id/curl is behaviourally impossible in normal operation, giving a very low-FP endpoint signal that complements the web-layer UC1. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@nocobase/plugin-notification-in-app-message/CVE-2026-52887/ • https://github.com/nocobase/nocobase/pull/9001
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Postgres archive_command / restore_command configured to call a shell script (WAL archiving)
  • PL/Perl or PL/Python stored procedures legitimately invoking helpers
  • DBA maintenance job using COPY TO PROGRAM for legitimate ETL/export
  • Container init or healthcheck script mis-parented under the postgres process tree
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "archive_command" and ProcessCommandLine !has "pg_wal"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child ProcessCommandLine — article shows payloads like 'id > /tmp/PWN_VERIFY.txt' and COPY reads of the users table; check the DB host /tmp for dropped files. 2) Contain: isolate the DB container, kill the spawned process tree, and rotate the exfiltrable secrets (users.password PBKDF2 hashes, admin id=1). 3) Hunt: correlate back to the originating web request (UC1) via timestamp, review any archive_command config to rule out benign use, and audit the postgres role for the rolsuper attribute that enabled COPY TO PROGRAM.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "postgres"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","cat","curl","wget","nc","ncat","chmod","python","python3","perl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has "postgres"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/id","/cat","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/python","/perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OctLurk/LurkProxy/SilkLurk C2 beacon to campaign-specific domains & VPS IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts endpoint DNS resolutions and network connections to the hard-coded C2 domains and VPS IPs published for the OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy Central Asia campaign (e.g. dns.multitoconference.com, dns.ssentialserv.xyz connectivity check, 154.196.162.76). These indicators uniquely identify the campaign's command-and-control channel and are shared with the SilentRaid/MystRodX/TrustFall infrastructure. Rationale: Uses the campaign's hard-coded C2 domains (dns.multitoconference.com OctLurk beacon, dns.ssentialserv.xyz LurkProxy connectivity check) and the 11 VPS IPs, three of which Kaspersky/STS confirm overlap with SilentRaid/MystRodX/TrustFall infrastructure — high-fidelity, cross-sourced indicators. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/01/china-linked-uat-7290-targets-telecoms.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

  • Security appliances/sandboxes detonating samples and generating the same C2 lookups
  • Threat-intel enrichment or DNS sinkhole services pre-resolving IOC domains
  • DNS logging proxies replaying historic queries during migration

Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process (InitiatingProcessFileName/ContextImageFileName) that resolved/connected to the IOC and whether the host is a Central Asian government/ministry asset in scope. 2) Contain: network-isolate the host, block the domain+IP at the firewall/DNS, and capture memory (both families run in-memory with a minimal on-disk loader). 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the loader on disk, secretsdump/fscan/pp.txt activity, an AnyDesk-named keylogger, and lateral net-use to admin shares; sweep the fleet for any other IOC-list domain or IP.

OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy/PlugX known sample hash execution or drop AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on process execution, image load, or file write matching the 16 MD5 hashes published for the OctLurk, SilkLurk, LurkProxy and side-loaded PlugX samples. Because both families are victim-specific and memory-resident, catching the minimal on-disk loader by hash is the cleanest execution-stage signal. Rationale: Directly uses the 16 published MD5s spanning OctLurk, SilkLurk, LurkProxy and side-loaded PlugX; hash IOCs are the highest-fidelity execution/install signal for memory-resident, victim-encoded loaders that otherwise leave minimal disk footprint. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://gbhackers.com/octlurk-and-silklurk-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1574.002 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analysts detonating the samples in a monitored analysis VM
  • AV/EDR quarantine copies retaining the file and re-triggering file events
  • Threat-intel researchers storing IOC samples on a corporate share
  • Hash collision is effectively nil for MD5 at this scale but re-used loader stub across benign packers is theoretically possible
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\\Sandbox\\", @"\\Analysis\\", @"\\Quarantine\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the hit is on a production endpoint (not an analysis sandbox) and record host, user, path and initiating process. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill/quarantine the sample, and capture volatile memory before reboot since the real payload lives in RAM. 3) Hunt: pull the loader's parent chain, look for the drive-serial/computer-name-keyed decode routine, and sweep for the C2 IOCs, secretsdump, fscan/pp.txt and AnyDesk-named keylogger across the estate.

Impacket secretsdump domain-controller hash extraction AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts command-line invocation of Impacket's secretsdump against domain controllers, matching the campaign's post-compromise step of harvesting password hashes from DCs. Anchors on secretsdump / -just-dc flags rather than LSASS access, so it complements existing credential-theft rules. Rationale: Article states hashes were harvested from domain controllers using Impacket's secretsdump.py; the secretsdump string plus -just-dc* flags are the tool's canonical invocation and rarely legitimate in production. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-backdoors-let-hackers-keylog/
ATT&CKT1003.006 T1003.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red-team / purple-team exercises legitimately running Impacket
  • AD security assessments using secretsdump for auditing
  • A pentest tool named similarly living in a security team's toolkit share
  • Detection engineering validating this very rule with an atomic test
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\\RedTeam\\" and DeviceName !in~ ("PENTEST-01","SECAUDIT-01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the source host/user is an authorized pentest asset; check the target (DC hostname) and whether -just-dc dumped NTDS. 2) Contain: disable the executing account, isolate the host, and treat all domain credentials as potentially compromised — begin krbtgt double-reset planning. 3) Hunt: correlate with the campaign C2 IOCs, look for prior remote-interactive logons to the DC, Pandora RC remote access, and subsequent lateral net-use to admin shares.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("secretsdump", "-just-dc-ntlm", "-just-dc-user", "-just-dc ")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| where CommandLine has_any ("secretsdump", "-just-dc-ntlm", "-just-dc-user", "-just-dc ")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
